catalog_quote: Phonetically Shanghai has seven tones, yin-p'ing, yang-p'ing, yin-shang, yin-ch'ü, yang-ch'ü, yin-ju and yang-ju. ... The phonological representation of Shanghai morphemes thus requires only four tones, namely p'ing, shang, ch'ü and ju. ... 2.5 Tone Change. The most conspicuous tone change in Shainghai [sic] is that of the yang-p'ing and the yang-ch'ü. The low rising pitch-contour of the yang-p'ing (which we indicate as 12) and the high rising pitch-contour of the yang-ch'ü (15) change into high falling unless the syllable carries primary stress. Shanghai composite nouns normally carry primary stress on their first syllables. Hence the following can be observed: zaŋ12-tʃĩn53 'the nerves' : tʃĩn53-zaŋ42 'spirits' ...
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Wu Chinese (wuch1236) is not in the catalog. this search of works with stress in the title had two title hits: Lyu 2018 (UW-Madison dissertation on Ningbo prosodic phonology, 457 pp.) and Selkirk & Shen 1990 (Prosodic domains in Shanghai Chinese, in Inkelas & Zec eds.). Neither text was obtainable: Lyu 2018 is ProQuest-only (not in MINDS@UW; only a one-sentence Google Books description and the abstract/reference list of the derived article Lyu 2019, IJCHL 6(1):119-161, doi:10.1075/ijchl.19004.lyu, were readable — both are about the tone-sandhi domain = prosodic word, silent on stress placement); Selkirk & Shen 1990 exists only as an access-restricted Internet Archive lending scan (phonologysyntaxc0000unse) and a Google Books partial preview (qt0f6KuNXmkC), neither readable by automated download, and it is not on the authors' homepages. Both items are 'unclear' for word stress (prosodic-domain/tone-sandhi studies of Wu varieties), both 'no-catalog-record', priority medium. As a lead outside the item list, Duanmu 1999 (JEAL 8:1-38, doi:10.1023/A:1008353028173, paywalled; abstract saved) treats Shanghai as a moraic-/disyllabic-trochee system where 'the initial syllable determines the tonal pattern of a multisyllabic domain' — the likeliest first-hand stress source for Shanghai Wu, but no page-located stress statement was read, so no new stress statement was found.org metadata and publisher pages.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Wu is a tone language (Shanghai: five citation tones, four phonological). Within a compound (the tone-sandhi domain) primary stress falls on the first syllable; only the stressed initial syllable keeps its underlying tone, and the non-initial syllables lose their own tones (Hashimoto's 'high falling' replacement; in Chen & Gussenhoven 2015 the initial tone determines the f0 contour of the whole tone unit). This is the left-headed (initial) stress account of Northern Wu formalised by Duanmu 1993/1995 and Chen 2000 (both paywalled) and restated by Wen 2026: 3.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned by Hashimoto. Edkins 1868: 18 notes 'a secondary accent on some other syllable in groups of three' (19th-century description; accent there said to prefer the last syllable).
new_statements.exceptions: Hashimoto: 'normally' - no explicit exception list. Contradicting/complicating evidence from the same language: Zhang 2006 (Shaoxing) says Shaoxing is right-prominent with an iambic stress foot (rightmost syllable of the foot is the head; trochaic only when the second syllable is an unstressed suffix such as the adjective marker [go?]); Wen 2026 finds no independent acoustic correlate of stress in Shaoxing and argues stress is inferred circularly from tone-sandhi dominance. Stress in Wu is therefore a phonological construct read off tone-sandhi patterns rather than an independently measured prominence.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the compound / tone-sandhi unit (polysyllabic word), not the phrase; monosyllabic words keep their citation tone. Left-dominant (initial) pattern is for Shanghai and the Taihu (Northern Wu) group generally; Southern Wu (e.g. Wenzhou) is right-dominant, and Shaoxing (Lin-Shao) is analysed as right-prominent by Zhang 2006. Chen & Gussenhoven 2015 note the lack of phrasal-level prominence as an open question.
new_statements.identity_note: Deciding quote describes the Shanghai dialect (Shanghainese, Glottolog shan1293, Taihu/Su-Hu-Jia group of Wu). The two other first-hand open sources (Zhang 2006, Wen 2026) describe Shaoxing (Glottolog Lin-Shao, lins1238; Zhang calls it 'southern Wu' but Glottolog places it in Taihu/Northern Wu) and give a different picture (right-prominent per Zhang; no independent evidence for stress per Wen). Wu is a dialect continuum; no single stress statement covers wuch1236 as a whole.

sources.citation: Wen, Xinyi. 2026. Phantom stress in tone sandhi: evidence from Shaoxing Wu Chinese. Amsterdam: LOT (LOT 724; Leiden PhD, defended 17 Sep 2026). 183 pp.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: pp. 2-3: 'Shanghai Wu is regarded as having left-headed word stress; the unstressed (i.e., non-initial) syllables undergo tonal deletion, while the underlying tone of the stressed syllable is preserved.. (e.g., M. Y. Chen, 2000; Duanmu, 1993, 1995)'. Sec. 5.2.1 pp. 110-111 (Shaoxing): 'we found no independent acoustic correlates of stress beyond tonal patterns themselves' (duration of disyllables: final syllable consistently longer regardless of sandhi type); 'our findings reveal no such independent evidence for stress in Shaoxing Wu'.
